original_question: Let f be a polynomial diffeomorphism of C^2 with Jacobian determinant delta, let U be a connected component of the interior of K^+(f), and suppose a subsequence of iterates on U converges to a rank-zero limit map g with g(U) = x_0. If the attracting fixed point x_0 lies on the boundary of U rather than in U, must one eigenvalue of Df at x_0 be equal to 1, with the other eigenvalue lying in the punctured unit disk D - {0}?
target_in_paper: §4, Stable regions for complex Hénon type maps (Milnor), specifically the Rank Zero Case on p. 10: the boundary subcase asking whether, when g(U) = x0 and x0 lies on the boundary of U, one multiplier must be 1 and the other must lie in the punctured open unit disk. ([math.stonybrook.edu](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/preprints/ims90-1.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the relevant setting and the right subproblem: a polynomial diffeomorphism f of C^2 with Jacobian determinant δ, a connected component U of int K^+(f), a subsequential Montel limit g of iterates on U, the rank-zero case g(U) = {x0}, and the specific boundary question about whether the eigenvalues at x0 must be 1 and a number in D - {0}. ([math.stonybrook.edu](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/preprints/ims90-1.pdf))
missing_details: The paper states this boundary question only in the nonwandering/periodic branch: if U is not a wandering component, then after replacing f by some finite iterate one assumes f(U) = U, and then f commutes with g. ([math.stonybrook.edu](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/preprints/ims90-1.pdf))

Because of that iterate-replacement, x0 is a fixed point of the replaced map f; before replacement, the corresponding point for the original map is only periodic. ([math.stonybrook.edu](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/preprints/ims90-1.pdf))

Your phrase 'attracting fixed point' is not paper-faithful in the boundary case. The paper says x0 is an attracting fixed point only when x0 lies in U; when x0 lies in ∂U, it instead conjectures that one eigenvalue is 1, so the point is not attracting in the usual strict sense. ([math.stonybrook.edu](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/preprints/ims90-1.pdf))
K^+(f) should be defined explicitly as the set of points with bounded forward orbit. ([math.stonybrook.edu](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/preprints/ims90-1.pdf))

The paper records that the limit rank is 0 or 1 only when |δ| < 1, while it is 2 if |δ| = 1; thus the rank-zero hypothesis implicitly places the question in the |δ| < 1 regime. ([math.stonybrook.edu](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/preprints/ims90-1.pdf))

For a fully stand-alone formulation, D should be defined as the open unit disk in C, so D - {0} means the punctured open unit disk. ([math.stonybrook.edu](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/preprints/ims90-1.pdf))

The paper phrases the conclusion in terms of the unordered eigenvalues of Df at x0: one eigenvalue must equal 1, and the other must lie in D - {0}. ([math.stonybrook.edu](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/preprints/ims90-1.pdf))
refined_question: Let f be a polynomial diffeomorphism of C^2 with constant Jacobian determinant δ, and let K^+(f) be the set of points with bounded forward orbit. Suppose U is a connected component of int K^+(f) that is not wandering; after replacing f by a suitable positive iterate, assume f(U) = U. Let g: U -> C^2 be a subsequential limit of the iterates f^n|U, and assume that g has rank 0, so g(U) = {x0}. If x0 lies in ∂U, must the eigenvalues of Df at x0 be {1, ν} with 0 < |ν| < 1?
justification: The draft is targeting the last sentence of the Rank Zero Case in §4, not the broader Question 1 and not the Rank One or Rank Two cases. The match is exact: the paper first introduces f, K^+(f), U, and the subsequential limit map g, then in the periodic reduction f(U) = U states the boundary conjecture that if x0 lies in ∂U, one eigenvalue should be 1 and the other should lie in D - {0}. The main corrections needed for paper-faithfulness are to add the nonwandering/iterate-replacement hypothesis and to remove the word 'attracting' from the boundary case. Also, the supplied arXiv item is a problem list, so the nearest official formulation is this informal Rank Zero Case question in §4 rather than a numbered theorem or proposition. ([math.stonybrook.edu](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/preprints/ims90-1.pdf))
